subtype: Approach: seeking professional support when low persists [Revision]
passage: Three months after the breakup, Jana noticed she was still not sleeping through the night, and her seminar notes had gone blank for weeks. For two months a heaviness had followed her from class to the library and back. Her flatmate Jamal said one evening, "It's been long. Maybe someone could help?" Jana had been telling herself to wait. This time she opened the university's website, found the counselling page and picked a time for Thursday. The counsellor in a small warm room did not hurry her. "It's good you came," they said. "Tell me what the last two months have been like." She talked for forty minutes. Walking out, she felt lighter, like someone had shared the weight.

qa.q: On which day did Jana book the counselling visit?
qa.a: Jana booked the visit for Thursday.

qa.q: What is Jana feeling as she leaves the counsellor's room?
qa.a: Jana feels lighter and supported, as though someone has shared the weight.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Jana add, and why?
qa.a: Jana could keep a few regular habits, such as meals and a short walk, because support from a counsellor works best alongside small steady routines.

qa.q: How might Jamal see Jana's decision?
qa.a: Jamal saw the long low stretch and gently suggested help, so Jamal is probably relieved that Jana acted instead of waiting.

grounding: Shows booking a campus counsellor visit when sadness stays heavy and affects study, instead of waiting longer.

subtype: Approach: seeking professional support when low persists [Revision]
passage:
The campus wellness centre had a fish tank and a box of tissues on every table. Aditi sat in the waiting room, knee bouncing, holding the appointment slip she'd booked online at midnight.
It had been two months since the breakup. She'd told herself it would pass. Instead she'd skipped nine classes, her mid-semester marks had dropped, and she felt heavy even on good days. Her friends had tried; she had stopped answering.
'Aditi?' A woman in a cotton sari smiled from a doorway. 'I'm Rukmini, one of the counsellors. Come in.'
Inside, Aditi said, 'I don't even know if this is serious enough to come here.'
'If you've felt this low since the breakup and your classes are suffering, that's reason enough,' Rukmini said. 'You don't have to wait until it's worse.'
They talked for fifty minutes. At the end, Aditi booked the next session for Thursday. Walking out, she felt, for the first time in weeks, that she wasn't carrying it alone.

qa.q: How many classes had Aditi skipped?
What was Aditi feeling in the waiting room?
qa.a: She was nervous and unsure, her knee bouncing, and doubted whether her sadness was serious enough to bring there.

qa.q: What else could Aditi do alongside the counselling?
qa.a: Reply to one friend who tried to help and say she has started seeing a counsellor, so support comes from more than one place.

qa.q: How does Rukmini see Aditi's worry about being 'serious enough'?
qa.a: Rukmini treats it as a common doubt and reassures Aditi that coming early is a good reason, not a failure.

grounding: Shows a student, low for two months with studies slipping, booking a campus counsellor instead of waiting, and starting to feel supported.

passage:
Dear Sonali,
You kept asking, and I kept saying 'I'm fine'. I wasn't. It's been nine weeks since Neel and I ended things. I thought I'd bounce back in a fortnight. Instead I stopped going to the library, I missed two assignment deadlines, and some mornings I just sat on my bed until lunch.
Last Monday my tutor asked, very kindly, if everything was okay. I nearly said 'fine' again. Instead I asked her how to see the college counsellor. She walked me to the office herself, and I booked a slot for that Wednesday.
The counsellor didn't tell me what to feel. She asked questions and let me talk, and for the first time in weeks I cried in front of someone. We've planned to meet every week for now.
I'm telling you because I don't want to keep pretending with you either. Chai this weekend?
Ishita

qa.q: How many assignment deadlines did Ishita miss?
What was Ishita feeling when the tutor asked if everything was okay?
qa.a: Ishita felt the pull to hide again but also some relief at being asked kindly, which gave the courage to ask for help.

qa.q: What could Sonali do after reading this?
qa.a: Say yes to chai, listen without trying to fix things, and keep checking in while Ishita continues the counselling.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel reading 'I don't want to keep pretending with you'?
qa.a: Sonali may feel sad about the weeks of 'I'm fine' but grateful and closer, now that Ishita has been honest.

grounding: Shows a student, low for weeks with studies slipping, asking about the campus counsellor rather than waiting and starting to feel supported.
